# Personas Core — shared practices

Practices the **Personas Core** workspace has adopted across its projects and that apply to this codebase. They are conventions to follow here unless this repo has a documented reason to differ — if you find such a reason, say so rather than silently diverging.

## api

### Choose the entry-point form by caller identity, not convenience _(proposed for this repo)_

Internal UI mutations and external callers need different things: the former wants type safety and no public URL, the latter needs a stable URL and raw-request access for signature verification. Split on caller identity, write the decision table down, and standardize the file naming — when the rule is convention-only, greppable naming is the entire enforcement.

docs/CULTURE.md principle #5 gives the decision table explicitly (UI→server work = Server Action; webhooks = Route Handler; public read API = Route Handler + API-key middleware; streaming AI = Route Handler since server actions can't stream). Enforcement is convention-only (no compile-time check) — the doc admits 'Mixed patterns metastasize fast' and standardizes naming (`actions.ts` per-feature, `*.action.ts` rejected) to keep the split grep-able.

### Close the outbound seam — the inbound one-door leaves it half done _(proposed for this repo)_

The inbound boundary is rigorously centralized while browser code calls the app's own routes from dozens of components, each re-implementing status branching, JSON parsing and error toasts. That asymmetry means the next contract change costs every component instead of one module.

grep found 26 non-test `fetch(` call sites across `src/components/**` and `src/features/**` (e.g. `src/components/employers/JobComposer.tsx:56,83,116,142`, `src/components/employers/PlacementBoard.tsx:199,224,274,313,323`, `src/features/placements/components/CandidateShortlist.tsx:142,167,582`). There is no `src/lib/api-client.ts` or equivalent wrapper — contrast with `src/lib/supabase/client.ts` which IS a single door for Supabase calls. This is a real structural asymmetry within the same repo: the inbound API boundary is rigorously centralized (guard.ts, auth-gate.ts) while the outbound boundary is ad hoc per-component, so a future contract change (e.g. new error shape) requires touching every component instead of one client module.

### Pick one validation idiom and make the wrapper demand it _(proposed for this repo)_

Hand-written parse functions that return a value or null keep validation beside the route and add no dependency, at the cost of shared schema tooling and type inference; a schema library trades the reverse. Either is defensible — what matters is that the request wrapper takes the validator as a required option so no route can skip validation, and that the codebase does not run both idioms at once.

`src/lib/api/guard.ts` GuardOptions type: `parse: (raw: unknown) => T | null; // Hand-rolled validator — repo idiom, NO zod.` grep for `z.object`/`from "zod"` across `src/` returns 0 hits, confirming this is consistently applied rather than a one-off. Every route wrapped by withApiGuard supplies its own `parse` + `invalidMessage`, keeping validation logic co-located with the route and dependency-free, at the cost of no shared schema/type-inference tooling.

### Wrap every route in one handler that owns errors and the envelope _(proposed for this repo)_

Response shape and error handling written per route drift into several dialects that every client must then understand. Wrap each route in one handler that catches thrown errors, logs them structurally, and coerces success and failure alike into a single typed envelope — the shape becomes a property of the layer rather than of whoever wrote the route.

`src/app/utils/apiErrorHandling.ts` defines `withApiHandler` (lines ~211-234) which wraps the handler, catches errors, and calls `wrapInEnvelope()` to normalize both success and legacy error shapes into `ApiEnvelope`. Routes call it directly: `src/app/api/characters/route.ts:15` — `export const GET = withApiHandler('GET /api/characters', async (request) => {...})`. `handleDatabaseError()` and `validateRequiredParams()` are shared helpers used by nearly every collection/detail route for Supabase error translation and required-field checks.

Counted via grep: `grep -rl withApiHandler src/app/api --include=route.ts | wc -l` → 62; total `route.ts` files → 67.

### Give the browser one typed request helper for your own routes _(proposed for this repo)_

Client components must reach the app's HTTP surface through a single request helper that owns timeouts, status-code branching and one typed error class, so callers branch on a named discriminator instead of re-deriving it from status codes. Per-component fetch with hand-rolled parsing and toasts is the same problem the inbound one-door already solved, left unfinished on the outbound side.

**Why this is one shared problem**

All four projects face the identical problem: browser code calling the app's own routes and needing consistent timeout, error and paywall/auth handling. The inbound side already has a one-door wrapper in most of them; the outbound side is the same problem in the same codebase and is simply unfinished in two of them — Apprenticeship Placement documents this as a gap against its own doctrine.

**Current approaches**

- **Local SEO Agency** — src/lib/apiClient.ts funnels every generation fetch through one request<T>() that always rejects with a single ApiClientError (status 0 = transport/timeout), exposing .isPaywall as the one discriminator callers branch on.
- **studio-story** — Per-entity TanStack Query integration hooks are the sole data-fetching layer, backed by a typed client error hierarchy (ApiError/TimeoutError/isNetworkError) and a useApiErrorHandler status→UX mapping hook.
- **Apprenticeship Placement** — No shared client; 26+ components call fetch('/api/...') directly, each re-implementing status branching, JSON parsing and error toasts.
- **ChainSonar** — Client components poll with bare fetch(...).then(r=>r.json()).catch(()

### Adapt rows into the UI shape once; never let one row break the list _(proposed for this repo)_

When a stored row shape and the frontend model diverge, write one directional adapter that always returns a valid object: shape-tolerant field access, every nested JSON parse wrapped, unrecognised values falling to a documented default. A malformed row then degrades to a dull entry instead of blanking the whole catalog.

`src/features/templates/sub_recipes/libs/recipeAdapter.ts` bridges the Rust `RecipeDefinition` row to the frontend `Recipe`. The module header states the direction and the reason ("the frontend type was written top-down for the recipe-redesign UX; the backend grew bottom-up out of Stage B's migration. Bridging them in one direction lets the existing browse / detail / adoption components consume real data without rewriting any of them").

The defensive vocabulary is small and reused everywhere:

```ts
function safeJsonArray<T>(raw: string | null | undefined): T[] { … try/catch → [] }
function asStringArray(arr: unknown[]): string[] { … typeof === 'string' && trim().length }
function nonEmptyString(v: unknown): string | undefined
```

`parsePromptTemplate` starts by building an `empty` result and returns it on any of: no prompt, non-object JSON, parse throw. Sub-shapes are accepted in multiple forms on purpose — `connectors` may be `string[]` or `{name}[]`; `suggested_trigger.trigger_type` is coerced into the narrower frontend union with `event_listener → webhook` and everything else to `manual`; `notification_channels` forwards only the recognised subset.

### Move a 'refresh all' loop server-side into one privileged call _(proposed for this repo)_

A 'test all' button implemented as a client-side fan-out over N privileged calls creates a stampede that can race the very session-token injection those calls depend on, reporting healthy resources as failures. Put the loop behind one call that runs it in process, share that implementation with the scheduled sweep so both persist results identically, and accept an indeterminate progress bar as the price.

`src-tauri/src/commands/credentials/crud.rs::healthcheck_all_credentials`:
> *"Doing the loop in one privileged call — instead of the frontend firing ~24 concurrent `healthcheck_credential` calls — removes the IPC stampede that raced the `x-ipc-token` injection and produced false "degraded" results. The client hook (`src/features/vault/shared/hooks/health/useBulkHealthcheck.ts`) documents the trade honestly: *"The server-side sweep doesn't stream per-credential progress, so the bar is effectively indeterminate: seed it with the visible count and snap to complete when the single call returns."* It also mirrors each returned result into the shared per-card health cache so the UI updates without a reload, and the API wrapper raises the timeout to 120s for this one call (`src/api/vault/credentials.ts`).

## architecture

### Route each cross-cutting concern through exactly one governed door _(proposed for this repo)_

A concern implemented at every call site can only be hardened at every call site. Give each one a single door — the IPC wrapper, the auth gate, the job manager, the process-spawn envelope — so timeouts, retries, instrumentation and enforcement live in one place. Below roughly three call sites it is not worth it, and one door accreting unrelated concerns has become a god module: one door per concern, not one door for everything.

**Practiced here:**
- invokeWithTimeout — the sole IPC door (timeout race · read-dedup · session-token retry) — lib/tauriInvoke.ts
- #[requires(auth|privileged|cloud)] proc-macro — one auth gate for every command — macros/src/lib.rs
- BackgroundJobManager<E> — 15+ scanner/compose commands share TTL/ring/stale-sweep — background_job.rs
- spawn_headless_claude — one LLM-spawn envelope (auth-strip · watchdog · line caps) — engine/cli_process.rs
- Event registry · error registry/taxonomy · repo layer · one execute-persona store method

**Limits — when NOT to apply**

A chokepoint concentrates change; if it starts accreting unrelated concerns it has become a god module — split by concern, keep one door *per concern*, not one door for everything. Not worth it below ~3 call sites.

### Make adding a variant one declarative edit against a registry _(proposed for this repo)_

When a new connector, nav section, event or template requires synchronized edits across several files, someone will eventually miss one and the omission is silent. Declare variants in a registry the code reads, and add a completeness check that fails the build when a variant is half-wired — the check is the payoff, so a registry without one buys little, and below three real variants a hand-wired switch is more honest.

**Practiced here:**
- Connector = a JSON contract, not code; a generic field-driven request builder consumes it — api_proxy.rs
- NAV_SECTIONS registry — adding a section is 2 files, compiler-enforced by a completeness test — lib/navigation/registry.ts
- Typed event registry · template category-folder catalog · DIM_REGISTRY scorecard · {minTier,devOnly} tier gate
- InjectionScope — a new memory-scoping axis is a 3-line change — repos/core/memories.rs

**Limits — when NOT to apply**

A registry below the rule of three (fewer than ~3 real variants) is premature abstraction; a hand-wired switch is honest until the third variant. The payoff is the completeness check, so a registry without one buys little.

### Derive route-keyed maps from the nav registry, not alongside it _(proposed for this repo)_

A second map keyed by the same union as the nav registry but authored independently is a registry in shape only: adding a section compiles cleanly while the parallel map silently lacks its entry. Either derive such maps from the registry or bring them under the same completeness check that governs it.

Violates **Extensibility is a declarative registry, not scattered wiring** (doctrine D2).

**Evidence**

`src/i18n/routeSections.ts:20-36` — `ROUTE_SECTIONS: Record<SidebarSection, readonly TranslationSection[]>`, a fourth independently-authored map keyed by the same union as the nav registry rather than derived from it.

### Depend on a module's boundary, never on its internals _(proposed for this repo)_

A module owns its internals; peers reach it through a declared surface, and data access stays behind its own layer — SQL behind repositories, UI primitives free of application state. Boundaries cost indirection, so a documented, deliberate exception beats one nobody believes in; the failure mode to fear is undocumented drift, not the exception itself.

**Practiced here:**
- sub_<concern> module map + a checked-in ownership table governs a 300-file feature — features/agents/AGENTS.md
- Repo-pattern boundary over the DB, generated by composable CRUD macros — db/macros.rs
- Shared-component catalog as a primitives boundary (no feature/app-state imports)

**Limits — when NOT to apply**

Boundaries have a cost in indirection and ceremony. A deliberate, documented exception (e.g. the companion treating markdown-on-disk as source of truth) beats a boundary nobody believes in — the failure mode is undocumented drift, not the exception itself.

### Stop peer features importing another feature's internal modals _(proposed for this repo)_

Detail and execution modals owned by one feature are imported directly by sibling features across several call sites, so the owning feature can no longer change its internals without breaking peers. Promote the shared surface into a boundary both sides can depend on instead of deepening the reach.

Violates **Enforce module boundaries and layering** (doctrine D4).

**Evidence**

`src/features/agents/sub_activity/ActivityModals.tsx:10-14` imports `@/features/overview/components/dashboard/widgets/DetailModal`, `@/features/overview/ExecutionDetailModal`, `@/features/overview/sub_events/EventDetailModal` — a peer feature reaching into another feature's internals (5+ import sites).

### Give the shared lib root a curated barrel instead of a flat drawer _(proposed for this repo)_

The top level of the shared library mixes domain directories, infrastructure, loose business logic and generated artifacts across dozens of entries with no curated entry point, unlike the hooks index and component catalog in the same repo. Nothing tells a newcomer which of it is public surface.

Violates **Enforce module boundaries and layering** (doctrine D4).

**Evidence**

`ls src/lib` → 65 top-level entries mixing domain dirs (analytics/, credentials/, errors/), infra (async/, config/), loose business logic, and generated artifacts (bindings/). No curated barrel — contrast `hooks/index.ts` and the component CATALOG.md.

### Give plugin panels one page contract the shell can host uniformly _(proposed for this repo)_

Each plugin panel is an independently shaped feature module defining its own page contract, so the shell cannot treat plugins as a single kind and every new plugin is bespoke wiring rather than an entry in a registry.

Violates **Enforce module boundaries and layering** (doctrine D4).

**Evidence**

### Write a cross-cutting contract down only if a test enforces it _(proposed for this repo)_

Ownership maps, dependency contracts and layering rules are worth checking in, but an artifact nobody verifies rots into a confident lie. Back each one with a compile-time guard, a replay test, or a CI diff gate so drift fails the build; if you cannot verify it, generate it from code instead of maintaining it by hand.

**Practiced here:**
- Idempotent migration framework — guarded steps + a 3× replay test asserting integrity — db/migrations/incremental.rs
- build_session README as a dependency-contract map over concern-clustered files; i18n four-layer CONTRACT.md
- ts-rs single-source bindings (build.rs → one dir) + a binding-drift verification gate
- Compile-time exhaustiveness guards — nav completeness test, draft field-group exhaustiveness

**Limits — when NOT to apply**

An artifact that is not machine-verified rots into a lie (see the AGENTS.md and checksum divergences below). Only write the contract down if you also add the test/CI gate; otherwise prefer generating it from code.

### Fix the template checksum gate's key contract before re-enabling it _(proposed for this repo)_

The manifest is keyed by full file path and hashes whole files while every caller passes a bare name and a payload, so the check passes vacuously for every adoption. This is tracked drift rather than an unknown hole — the earlier hard-reject variant bricked the feature in release builds — so repair the key and content contract instead of simply switching rejection back on.

Violates **Make the contract an artifact — and make it verifiable** (doctrine D5).

**Evidence**

`src-tauri/src/commands/design/template_adopt.rs:25-58` — manifest is keyed by full file path + hashes the whole file; every caller passes a bare name + payload-only JSON, so `is_known_template` is false for 100% of adoptions. **Important nuance: this is documented, tracked drift, not an unknown hole** — the inline comment records that the previous hard-reject variant *bricked the entire Presets + Dev Clone feature in release builds*, so the check was deliberately downgraded to a warn pending manifest reconciliation. Fix the key/content contract; do NOT simply re-enable the reject.

### Generate the module ownership table instead of hand-maintaining it _(proposed for this repo)_

The checked-in ownership map omits several real modules including a very large one, so the map that is supposed to govern the directory has drifted from it. An unverified hand-written map is precisely the failure the repo's own contract doctrine warns about.

Violates **Make the contract an artifact — and make it verifiable** (doctrine D5).

### Make the prompt/gate keyword pairing compiler-enforced _(proposed for this repo)_

The build session's prompt and its gate machine agree on a keyword set only by hand, so adding a keyword on one side silently desynchronises the other and the gate stops firing. Derive both from one declaration, or add an exhaustiveness check that fails compilation.

Violates **Make the contract an artifact — and make it verifiable** (doctrine D5).

**Evidence**

The build-session prompt/gate keyword pairing is a hand-maintained contract with no compiler enforcement — a keyword added to one side silently desyncs the gate machine.

### Restrict cross-feature imports to public barrels, checked by a test _(proposed for this repo)_

Deep imports between features couple peers to each other's file layout, so any internal reorganisation becomes a cross-feature change. Enforce barrel-only cross-feature imports with a real restricted-import rule, exempt type-only imports since they erase at build time, verify the rule by running the actual lint config against fixtures rather than trusting the documentation, and state which trees are not yet covered.

`src/architecture/barrel-imports.lint.test.ts` (ADR 0019/0029): loads the real `eslint.config.mjs` via the ESLint Node API and asserts deep cross-feature imports trip `@typescript-eslint/no-restricted-imports` (lines 29-43) while barrel imports (45-51), type-only imports (53-59), and intra-feature relative imports (61-67) pass. Test also documents current scope gaps explicitly: "rule is scoped to features — a composition-root deep import is NOT flagged here ... src/services is intentionally out of scope for this increment (follow-up)" (lines 69-76) — an honest, tracked boundary gap rather than a silent one.

### Enforce load-bearing invariants with branded types, not runtime checks _(proposed for this repo)_

Tenant isolation, citation verification and sign-off state are invariants an outbound function must never violate, and a runtime check only catches the violation after the code exists. Encode them as branded types whose only constructor is the function that performs the check, keep the unsafe minting helper internal and out of the barrel, and unverified or unsigned artifacts stop compiling rather than failing review.

src/lib/citations/types.ts:8-32 — `VerifiedLegalText = string & {[VerifiedBrand]:true}`; `_unsafeBrand()` is documented '@internal', lives only in verify.ts, 'never exported from the package barrel... If you find yourself reaching for this, you are about to undermine CULTURE.md §3.' docs/CULTURE.md principles #1/#3/#4 describe the analogous pattern for `TenantContext` (Map<TenantId,Map<Id,T>> makes cross-tenant reads physically impossible) and `Signed<T>` (phantom brand, `_unsafeSign()` internal-only, state machine drafted→in_review→signed→delivered with a `revision_requested` branch back to drafted).

### Pass cross-feature enrichment as an optional parameter _(proposed for this repo)_

When one feature's output enriches another's work, importing across features from inside the core logic couples them permanently. Take the enrichment as an optional parameter so the consumer degrades gracefully when it is absent, and let the action layer decide what context to inject — keeping the core pure and independently testable.

docs/CULTURE.md 'Cross-feature data flow via optional enrichment': `buildDemandPrompt(facts: MatterFacts, chronology?: string)` — absent chronology means the base prompt ships without a chronology section; the action layer decides. `src/features/demand-letter/actions.ts:26-49` shows the concrete cross-feature import surface (matters, medical-records, settlement, sign-off) all composed at the action layer rather than the prompt/store layers reaching across features directly.

### Split crates along data-flow stages, one job per crate _(proposed for this repo)_

Crates split by technical layer end up depending on each other in both directions; crates split along the pipeline's stages do not. Give each crate a single responsibility mirroring a stage, keep the crate root a short index of re-exports with no logic in it, and open each with a doc comment naming its one job and the architecture section it implements.

`Cargo.toml:3-12` workspace members list; `crates/brainiac-pipeline/src/lib.rs:1-7` — "the ingest -> extract -> embed -> resolve -> contradict -> promote chain (ARCHITECTURE.md section 3)"; `crates/brainiac-store/src/lib.rs:1-11` opens with the RLS connection-discipline doctrine before any code. Every crate's lib.rs is a short index (16-35 lines) that only declares `pub mod` and re-exports — no logic lives at the crate root.

### Let each feature own its types, storage, validation and components _(proposed for this repo)_

Domain logic scattered between routes and shared utilities has no obvious home, so it lands wherever the current task happens to be. Give each business domain a directory that owns its types, persistence wrapper, validation and components behind a barrel, keep cross-cutting infrastructure in shared modules imported by features and never the reverse, and leave the route layer as glue.

Directory sample: `src/features/drafts/{computation,lookup,storage,types,validation}.ts` + `index.ts` barrel; `src/features/grant-explorer/{data,filter,search,labels,index-cache,types}.ts`. Cross-cutting concerns (auth, db, llm, rate-limit, tokens, server-action) live under `src/lib/*` and are imported by features, never the reverse. `src/app/drafts/[grantId]/actions.ts` and `page.tsx` are the route glue that call into `src/features/drafts/storage.ts` and `@/lib/tokens/guard`.

### Isolate every event subscriber with its own timeout and error boundary _(proposed for this repo)_

An in-process bus attached to the store lets mutations publish domain events without knowing their consumers, but a throwing or slow subscriber must never break the mutation or its siblings. Race each handler against a timeout, report failures through an error hook that is itself wrapped, and state the scope — single process, no durability — explicitly so nobody mistakes it for a queue.

`src/lib/events/bus.ts:1-11` scopes the design explicitly as in-memory/single-process by design (durability/fan-out deferred, see ADR-0007). `#runHandler` (lines 54-75) races the handler promise against a `setTimeout` rejection at `DEFAULT_HANDLER_TIMEOUT_MS=5000`; `publish()` (98-125) wraps each handler dispatch's error reporting itself in try/catch so a throwing `onError` reporter can't break the `Promise.all` isolation guarantee. Consumers: `src/lib/events/subscribers/attorney-notify.ts` and `audit-log.ts`.

### Keep route files to metadata and mounting one feature component _(proposed for this repo)_

Once a route file holds UI logic, that logic is reachable only through the URL that owns it. Keep every route a thin shell that resolves metadata and mounts the feature component, so the same feature can be composed, tested and relocated without touching routing.

`app/hlasovani/page.tsx` is 18 lines: metadata + `const themeData = await getVoteThemes(); return <VoteTrackPage themeData={themeData} />;`. CLAUDE.md states the convention directly: "Routes stay thin — a page.tsx only mounts a feature and sets metadata" and labels the whole `Code structure` section "patterns adopted from the personas repo."

### Make each use case a crate implementing one trait over a shared core _(proposed for this repo)_

When every use case is an independent crate implementing a single trait and all shared machinery lives in a core crate, adding one is purely additive: create the crate, declare it, register one line. Document that checklist next to the registry and glob the workspace members, so existing crates never have to be edited to admit a new one.

`crates/core/src/app.rs:421-449` defines `ScrapeApp` (`name`, `schedule`, `requires`, `default_params`, `run(ctx: AppContext)`). `crates/server/src/registry.rs:1-11` documents the whole integration contract in a doc-comment: "1. create a crate under crates/apps/<name> ... 2. add it to [workspace.dependencies] ... 3. add one line here", then lists 20 `Arc::new(app_X::X)` entries. Cargo.toml workspace members use a glob (`crates/apps/*`) so new app crates are picked up without touching the root manifest structure.

### Expose metered capabilities only as methods on a context object _(proposed for this repo)_

Handing application code the raw engines means unmetered calls, and cost accounting silently under-reports rather than failing. Expose every side-effecting capability as a method on one context object that meters, budget-checks and records learned routing in a single place — and if an escape hatch must exist, document that whoever uses it owes the accounting themselves.

`crates/core/src/app.rs:190-298` — `AppContext::fetch` wraps `engines.fetch.fetch`, adds learned-tier skip logic (`tiers.preferred`), budget-clamps `AutoWithResearch`, then always calls `self.meter(...)` and `self.learn_tier(...)` before returning. `AppContext::research` (line 306-332) is the same pattern for Claude calls: cache lookup, budget guard, meter, cache write. The doc-comment on `meter` (line 147-153) states explicitly: apps that must drive an engine raw (the crawler) must call `meter`/`learn_tier` themselves or become invisible to cost/budget accounting — i.e. the chokepoint is a convention apps can escape, but doing so is a conscious, documented trade.

### Define the plugin trait in core, keep the runtime in its own crate _(proposed for this repo)_

A sandbox runtime dependency in the shared crate is paid for by everything that depends on it. Declare only the plugin trait plus a null-object fallback in core and keep the actual runtime in a separate crate, so the shared crate never compiles the sandbox and disabling plugins returns a typed error instead of panicking.

`crates/core/src/plugin.rs:1-11` module doc: "core defines only the trait; the wasmtime dependency lives in engine-wasm so the runtime stays out of the shared crate." `Plugins::run` takes `params: &Value` so one compiled WASM module can be reused across jobs/configs instead of recompiling per variation (lines 19-24). `NoPlugins` (lines 43-56) is the fallback when plugins are disabled, returning a typed `Error::App` rather than panicking.

### A door that only convention protects is not a chokepoint _(proposed for this repo)_

Once a governed door exists, the only remaining question is what stops the next call site from skipping it. Enforce it mechanically — restricted-import zones, type-level operation registries, boundary tests — and make any deliberate bypass an enumerated, tested exception list rather than an open escape hatch, because a self-documented leak is still a leak.

**Why this is one shared problem**

The portfolio has overwhelmingly converged on the one-door pattern, so the remaining question is identical everywhere: what stops the 63rd route from skipping it. Three projects answered with enforcement and three carry live, self-documented leakage — that is a maturity gap in one shared practice, not a difference in problem.

**Current approaches**

- **ai-paralegal** — Every model call goes through callAI(); a flat-config no-restricted-imports rule bans @google/generative-ai outside src/lib/ai/**, so the boundary is physically enforced.
- **Local SEO Agency** — Concrete drivers (firebase-admin, pg, PGlite) are banned outside the persistence zone by an ESLint zone, and src/lib/boundaries.test.ts asserts the rule still holds.
- **ai-bookkeeper** — Cross-feature imports are restricted to each feature's public barrel by a real lint rule, verified by a characterization test that runs the actual eslint config against fixtures — while explicitly documenting that src/services is not yet covered.
- **Pumper** — AppContext is the sole metered door, but roughly half the app crates call ctx.engines.http.fetch(...) directly, bypassing cost meter

### Sequence auth, metering, validation and shaping once per request _(proposed for this repo)_

Re-implementing the request preamble per route guarantees that some route eventually does it in the wrong order, and that ordering bug is invisible until it is exploited. Sequence auth, metering, validation, logging and response shaping once inside a single wrapper or context object every handler passes through, so the concern becomes hardenable and enforceable in one place.

### Keep one transport subscription and fan out to components in JS _(proposed for this repo)_

A hot event stream consumed by many components should not open one transport subscription per consumer. Hold exactly one and fan out in application code: buffer events that arrive before the first subscriber mounts with a cap and a drop counter the subscriber can see, dispatch once per animation frame so the framework batches them into a single render, and guard the race where every subscriber unmounts while the subscribe call is still resolving.

`src/hooks/realtime/createSingletonListener.ts` returns a hook; regardless of how many components use it there is one `listen(eventName)`.

- **Early buffer** — events arriving with zero subscribers go into `earlyBuffer` up to `MAX_BUFFER = 50`; overflow increments `earlyDroppedCount` and warns exactly once. A subscriber that mounts later is told about drops that happened before it existed.
- **Frame coalescing** — "a single backend tick can land multiple payloads within the same animation frame ... Collecting them and dispatching once per frame keeps React commits aligned with paint and lets React 18's automatic batching collapse N events into one render." The buffer drain routes through the same frame queue "so a large early-buffer drain doesn't saturate the microtask checkpoint with one render-per-event".
- **Setup/teardown race** — `setupInFlight` guards the window where all subscribers unmount while `listen()` is still resolving; the setup completion handler unlistens immediately if `subscribers.size === 0`.

The complementary per-component hook, `src/hooks/useTauriEvent.ts`, encodes the async-subscription cleanup race explicitly (a `cancelled` flag plus calling the unli

_(evidence truncated)_

### Give a multi-section editor one dirty/save registry, wired via refs _(proposed for this repo)_

Sections that each own their dirty flag and save routine cannot be saved, cancelled or undone as one document. Put dirty state, save and cancel callbacks and the undo stack in a single external store that sections self-register into — and register a stable trampoline that dereferences a ref at call time, because under concurrent rendering a discarded render can otherwise leave the registry pointing at aborted state.

`src/features/agents/sub_editor/libs/EditorDocument.tsx` builds a plain `createDirtyStore()` (maps for dirty/save/cancel, listener set, undo+redo stacks, memoized `getDirtyTabs` for referential stability) behind `EditorDirtyProvider`, consumed by `useEditorDirtyState()` / `useEditorHistory()` via `useSyncExternalStore`. `PersonaEditor.tsx` is nothing but the provider wrapping `EditorBody`.

Sections opt in through one config object (`src/features/agents/sub_editor/libs/useTabSection.ts`): `{ tab, isDirty, save, mode: 'debounced' | 'immediate' | 'explicit', delay, deps, enabled }`. It wires the debounce, registers with the store, and auto-unregisters on unmount.

The ref-trampoline detail is a recorded React 19 fix:

> "Previously these were registered directly during render with the comment 'registerSave/registerCancel do not call notify(), so updating during render is safe' — but under React 19 Concurrent rendering a discarded render would still leave the registry pointing at a closure that captured aborted state, so a subsequent saveAll could persist values the user never saw."

### Group look-alike panels by data tier and commit the routing rubric _(proposed for this repo)_

Panels that all render 'what the system is doing' look identical but consume different data tiers and answer different questions, so they get filed by appearance and the tree-rendering logic is duplicated. Name the tiers, declare the direction data flows between them, and commit a numbered decision rubric plus an anti-pattern list in the folder so the next panel lands in the right place.

`src/features/overview/README.md` opens with the cost it is preventing: "They look similar (timelines, trees, badges) but consume **three different data sources** and serve **three different user questions**. Putting a panel in the wrong folder is the leading cause of duplicated tree-rendering logic in this codebase."

It then draws the tiers with their model type, grouping key and user question:

| tier | model | grouped by | question |
|---|---|---|---|
| live event bus (in-memory, <1s) | `RealtimeEvent` | `chainId` | "Is the system alive right now?" |
| durable event log (SQLite) | `PersonaEvent` | user's filter | "Find me the event where X happened yesterday." |
| trace + healing | `UnifiedSpan` / `SystemTrace` | `traceId` | "What went wrong, what's the root cause, is the healer on it?" |

"Data flows left-to-right... Never reach across tiers in the opposite direction (e.g. do not render a trace span tree from realtime events — use the trace engine)."

## auth

### Decide access in a pure function; keep persistence separate _(proposed for this repo)_

Delegated-access logic that reads grants from the database inline can only be tested with a database and can only be reviewed by tracing queries. Split it: one dependency-free module resolves the scope decision from grants plus an injected clock as plain data, and a second module owns persistence of grants and the access log. Any externally supplied owner identifier must pass through that decision before a per-owner query runs, and a regression sweep should assert it.

`src/lib/auth/access.ts:1-70`: "Pure — no DB, no I/O — so the scope resolution + grant lifecycle rules are unit-testable like session/ledger." `resolveAccess(viewerUserId, ownerUserId, grants, nowMs)` takes `nowMs` injected rather than reading a clock (deterministic tests). CLAUDE.md: "Isolation is app-layer only (no RLS): any query on a per-owner table needs its owner_id/user_id WHERE clause; external ownerId params must be gated by resolveAccessForViewer + canRead/canExport first. Regression sweep: src/lib/data/owner-isolation.test.ts."

### Fail open in dev and closed in production behind one predicate _(proposed for this repo)_

Keyless dev and demo builds need auth and metering to degrade gracefully, but the same missing configuration in production must be a hard failure rather than a free pass. Express the degradation as one predicate used on both sides, paired with startup assertions that throw when the production condition is met. The request-time gate and any user-facing indicator must read the same predicate, or the UI promises something the API does not honour.

`src/lib/api/auth-gate.ts` `requireUserWhenAuthConfigured()` returns `{ok:false, 503 auth_not_configured}` in production when auth isn't configured, but proceeds with `user=null` outside production. `src/lib/tokens/guard.ts` mirrors this with `assertBypassNotInProduction()` and `assertMeteringConfiguredInProduction()`, and documents the invariant explicitly: "`isUnmeteredContext()`... and the header balance pill (`getBalanceForViewer`) MUST agree on this predicate, so the pill's ∞ never disagrees with what the API actually charges." This is a repeated repo-wide idiom (grep shows the same fail-open-dev/fail-closed-prod shape reused across auth, tokens, and DB config checks) rather than a one-off.

### Make the database enforce tenancy by demoting the app's role _(proposed for this repo)_

Row-level policies do nothing if the application connects as an owner or superuser, because those roles bypass them by design. Demote every pooled connection to a non-owner role at connect time so policies structurally apply to all runtime queries, and set the tenant scope as transaction-local configuration inside a scoped transaction so it can never leak onto a pooled connection reused by another request. Any wider read path (a pipeline worker) should be a separate, named, documented escape hatch — never the default.

`crates/brainiac-store/src/lib.rs:1-11` (doc), `:83-98` (`connect` demotes role), `:100-123` (`scoped_tx` sets LOCAL config). A second `worker_tx` grants org-wide (never-private) read via an `app.worker` escape hatch documented at migration `0002_worker_read.sql`, used only by pipeline stages, never end-user request paths.

### Split bootstrap tokens from scoped managed tokens _(proposed for this repo)_

A service needs an operator break-glass credential that works before any database row exists, and it needs per-customer credentials that are scoped and revocable — conflating the two makes one of the requirements impossible. Resolve a bearer against a static environment map first with no I/O, then fall through to hashed managed tokens with per-token scopes and revocation. Define clearly what an unscoped bootstrap token means and which scope implies the others, so the check is one function rather than per-endpoint reasoning.

`crates/brainiac-server/src/auth.rs:1-14` (doc), `:126-133` (`allows`), `:152-188` (`resolve_bearer`). The `SCOPES` const at `:97-110` carries an explicit incident writeup: `kb:*`/`lib:*` scopes were enforced on endpoints before being added to this vocabulary list, so a token minted with `lib:read` was rejected as out-of-vocabulary and only `admin` tokens could reach the endpoint — collapsing least-privilege into all-or-nothing. Fixed, and the store's own pg tests were widened to mint through the real endpoint instead of bypassing validation via `brainiac_store::tokens::create` directly.

### Keep the mintable scope vocabulary and enforcement in one place _(proposed for this repo)_

When scopes are enforced ad hoc per endpoint but must also appear in a central list to be mintable, the list becomes a second source of truth that drifts silently. An enforced scope missing from the vocabulary produces an endpoint that looks governed but is reachable only by an admin token — least privilege collapsed into all-or-nothing, discovered when onboarding a real customer. Mint through the real endpoint in tests, not through the store function, or the validation gap ships.

`crates/brainiac-server/src/auth.rs:79-96` documents the incident directly in the doc comment above `pub const SCOPES`, including how it was found (`load/README.md F-1`, a customer-onboarding attempt) and the test-gap that let it ship (pg tests minted tokens through the store function directly, bypassing the validation the real `/v1/tokens` endpoint enforces).

### Name every table that sits outside your RLS boundary _(proposed for this repo)_

A codebase that enforces tenancy through scoped transactions for its core tables usually also has an operational set — job queues, tokens, projects, onboarding requests — reached through the raw pool with the tenant identifier threaded by hand. That split can be deliberate, but describing the raw path as 'non-tenant' when genuinely org-scoped data flows through it misleads the next maintainer into trusting a boundary that is not there. Document the exceptions by name, or move them inside the boundary.

`crates/brainiac-store/src/lib.rs:143-146` documents `pool()` as "raw pool access for non-tenant subsystems (the job queue)" — but the actual call sites extend well beyond the queue: `crates/brainiac-server/src/http.rs:575,1435,1515,1563` and `projects.rs:279,401` all call `.pool()` directly for org-scoped reads/writes, passing `ctx.principal.org_id` manually rather than opening a `scoped_tx`. This is likely deliberate (these tables may not carry RLS policies at all, unlike memories/documents), but the doc comment's framing ("non-tenant") undersells how much genuinely org-scoped data flows through the unscoped path — a maintainer skimming the lib.rs doctrine could reasonably assume `pool()` never touches tenant data, which is not true.

### Resolve the tenant once at the request boundary and thread it down _(proposed for this repo)_

Multi-tenancy retrofitted onto a single-user schema usually means rewriting every query; making the organization identifier the owner's own user identifier avoids that entirely, since already-scoped queries are shared by construction. Resolve the active tenant once per request at the framework boundary from the session plus a cookie validated against the caller's membership set, then thread the value down into storage code that stays session-agnostic and unit-testable. Ignore a forged cookie, and fail fast rather than silently falling back to a shared default org.

`src/lib/auth/org.ts:9-24` comment: "Scope-first multi-tenancy: an org's id IS its OWNER's user id. A solo user is their own org... a user who has joined a team resolves to the owner's id... Resolved ONLY at the RSC/Server Action boundary; the value is threaded down into the session-agnostic storage layer so feature modules stay pure and unit-testable (no server-only import in feature code)." The cookie is validated against `listMembershipsForUser` inside `resolveActiveOrgId` — an explicit IDOR guard (line 36-37: "a forged/non-member cookie is ignored"). Falls back to `DEFAULT_PROFILE_ID` only in the keyless/unconfigured-auth case; with a configured provider and no user, it throws `MissingSessionError` rather than silently scoping to the shared default org (lines 48-61) — deliberately fail-fast over a tenant-isolation footgun.

### Express route authorization as one composable fail-closed policy _(proposed for this repo)_

Hand-rolled per-route ownership checks diverge, and the divergence is where cross-tenant reads slip through. Replace them with a single authorization function taking a small policy object, where opting into a cross-tenant fallback is an explicit flag that fails closed when its configuration is unset. Never gate that fallback on a demo or presentation flag — conflating a UI unlock with an authorization predicate is the classic fail-open, data-egress bug.

`src/lib/auth/authorizeRoute.ts:87-96` docstring: 'Cross-tenant access gates on isConfiguredAttorney... NEVER isAttorney (the demo unlock) — the HIGH auth-fail-open / PII-egress class the team gated before release.' The owner match (`getCaseForUser`) always wins outright; the attorney fallback (`getCaseAnyOwner`) is only consulted when both `policy.requiresAttorney` AND `isConfiguredAttorney(user.email)` hold (lines 113-122). Body is read via `request.clone().json()` since the body is single-consumption and the calling route re-parses it for its own payload (lines 70-85).

### Treat an auth-provider flip as a session drain, not a config toggle _(proposed for this repo)_

When an app supports two auth backends behind one active-provider switch, the session reader only understands the currently selected medium — so flipping the switch makes every live session of the other medium invisible at once, with no error and no log to correlate. That is a silent mass logout, and it will be reported as an outage. If the risk is accepted, write it down at the switch and treat any production provider change as a planned drain of existing sessions.

`src/lib/auth/session.ts:73-81` comment (labeled 'auth-session #2'): 'Live sessions of BOTH media can coexist in users' browsers, so changing the active provider... makes every existing session of the OTHER medium invisible — a silent mass-logout with no log to correlate. This is accepted today (single global switch). If you change the active provider in prod, DRAIN existing sessions first.' A dual-auth-backend project should treat provider migration as a planned drain, not a config toggle.

### Size the auth model to the operator count, and say when it's unset _(proposed for this repo)_

A single-operator console does not need accounts and sessions; a shared secret compared at the one write path is the simplest correct choice, and pretending otherwise adds a surface to maintain and to get wrong. What matters is honesty about configuration: return an explicit not-configured result distinct from unauthorized, so the UI renders a real read-only state instead of a write path that cannot work. Validate enumerated inputs at the boundary too, since types are erased there.

`features/money/reviewActions.ts:9-17` states the rationale directly: "single-operator console, simplest correct choice for this batch." Result union at lines 34-39 has 5 explicit states (`ok|not-configured|unauthorized|not-found|error`) rather than a boolean, so every caller path is distinguishable. A runtime whitelist check (`VALID_DECISIONS.includes(input.decision)`) guards against TS-type-erasure at the server-action boundary (comment cites "D5 batch 004").

### Make tenant scope structurally unforgettable, not per-call discipline _(proposed for this repo)_

Every multi-tenant system fails the same way: one new query that forgets the filter. Put isolation in a seam that cannot be skipped — a database-enforced policy, or a scope argument the type system requires as the first parameter of every domain function — so a new query or route cannot silently produce a cross-tenant read. Per-route authorization functions and manually threaded tenant identifiers should be the documented exception, not the default; this portfolio already contains a case where the weaker form leaked.

**Why this is one shared problem**

Five members are multi-tenant and all face the same failure mode: one new query that forgets the filter. The stack differs (Postgres vs Firestore) but the doctrine does not, and the portfolio contains a proof that the weaker form leaks in practice — brainiac's own harvest records that its operational tables sit outside the RLS boundary it built for its knowledge tables.

**Current approaches**

- **brainiac** — Store::connect demotes every pooled connection to a non-owner brainiac_app role so RLS structurally applies — but operational tables (job queue, tokens, projects) are reached via raw pool() with org_id threaded manually as a bound parameter.
- **ai-paralegal** — TenantContext is a branded type with a private constructor required as the first argument of every domain function, and FeatureStore is tenant-scoped on every call — enforcement at compile time.
- **Grant Writing Nonprofits** — Org id IS the owner's user id, resolved once per request at the RSC/Action boundary by getActiveOrgId(), so already-org-scoped queries need no rewrite — correct by construction but dependent on callers using the resolver.
- **Immigration Paperw

_(evidence truncated)_

### Enumerate expensive scopes per resource and time-box by default _(proposed for this repo)_

Issued API keys drift toward one blanket capability because enumerating targets is friction at creation time — and that blanket capability is what an exfiltrated key monetizes. Split capabilities into cheap toggles and expensive ones that must be named per resource, and make enabling the expensive one without picking a target a blocking validation error so no path to a blanket grant exists. Offer a never-expiring option if you must, but default the expiry to a finite window, and apply the mirror rule to inbound pairing requests.

`src/features/settings/sub_api_keys/components/CreateApiKeyDialog.tsx`:

```ts
const AVAILABLE_SCOPES = [ 'personas:build', 'personas:read' ];  // simple toggles
...
const scopes = [
  ...selectedScopes,
  ...(allowExecute ? [...executeIds].map((id) => `personas:execute:persona:${id}`) : []),
];
```

Enabling execute without picking any target is a blocking validation error (`error_execute_persona_required`), so there is no path to a blanket execute scope. `EXPIRY_OPTIONS` are `[7, 30, 90, never]` with state initialised to `90` — never-expiring is reachable but is not the default. `PairApprovalModal` applies the mirror-image rule on the inbound side: the requesting origin's scopes are rendered as individually deselectable checkboxes plus a 7/30/90-day expiry, and non-HTTPS origins get a visible warning.

## billing

### Wrap every metered route in one envelope owning the four concerns _(proposed for this repo)_

Auth, metering, billing telemetry and structured logging repeat verbatim in every metered AI route, and each hand-rolled copy drifts. Put them in one wrapper that sequences them in a fixed order — logging, then auth independent of metering, then charge-with-reclaim around the handler — and hand the handler a clean context so it never re-implements the reject ladder.

`src/lib/tokens/guard.ts:241-318`, doc comment: "Wraps a handler with the four concerns every insight route repeated verbatim". Session is resolved once (`requireUser()` then reused by `chargeForOperation`, no duplicate `getUser()`). Fail-closed posture: `meteringMode()` free-passes only outside production; in production an unconfigured auth/DB '`deny`'s rather than serving AI for free (lines 56-73). CLAUDE.md also documents this as the mandated pattern ("Metered API routes use withMeteredRoute ... Inline chargeForOperation is allowed only for categorize's anonymous demo path") — i.e. one named, intentional exception.

### Debit before the model call, refund on every failure path _(proposed for this repo)_

Metered work must debit the ledger before the provider call, so a caller who cannot pay never reaches the model. Every failure path — a handler throw, a degraded response with no billable value, a rate-limit race that fills the window mid-charge — must issue a best-effort, idempotent refund keyed to the original charge, and that refund must never throw and mask the real error.

`src/lib/tokens/guard.ts:40-47` doc: "Call at the top of an AI route. Debits upfront (charge-then-reclaim) ... On success returns a reclaim() to call if the downstream operation throws." Race handling at lines 118-125: rate-limit window can fill during the `await charge()`; if so the just-made charge is refunded and the request rejected 429 "so a serviced slot and a charged token never diverge." Reclaim also releases the user's rate-limit slot (lines 144-147) so failed zero-cost reads don't lock a user out.

### Cap the request body before the charge, not after it _(proposed for this repo)_

Compose the metered route's door as one fixed pipeline: body-size cap, parse, shape validation, charge, handler, reclaim-on-throw. The cap belongs before the charge specifically, so a caller cannot amplify a flat per-operation price into an arbitrarily large model invocation, and one shared error mapping keeps every endpoint's failure shape identical.

`src/lib/api/guard.ts:120-140` describes the pipeline explicitly: "1. body-size cap → 413 (M1: before any charge) 2. JSON parse → 400 3. shape validate → 400 4. charge → 401/402 5. handler → 200, with idempotent reclaim-on-throw". The 16KB body cap (`MAX_BODY_BYTES`, guard.ts:73) is applied BEFORE the metered LLM call specifically so a caller can't amplify a flat per-op charge into an arbitrarily large model invocation (comment attributes this to a security-sentinel pre-implementation audit finding, "M1"). `llmErrorResponse()` (guard.ts:20-31) is the single canonical mapping of a transient LLM failure to HTTP (429 rate-limit / 500 outage), shared by withApiGuard AND the one hand-rolled route that couldn't use it (`/api/compliance/report`), so every metered endpoint returns the same `{error: 'rate_limited'|'llm_unavailable'}` shape.

### Arm auto-reclaim on the abort signal, and disarm it on settle _(proposed for this repo)_

A client that disappears between the debit and the delivered stream must be refunded, but a disconnect after the work was saved must not be. Register a once-guarded auto-reclaim on the request's cancellation signal at charge time and disarm it the moment billable work is persisted, refunding synchronously when the request was already cancelled on entry.

`charge-route.ts:56-134`. Key mechanics: already-aborted-at-entry is refunded synchronously (`await safeReclaim()`) before returning a 499, "AWAITED, so a process/connection teardown can't drop the credit" (lines 109-117); partial-refund support via a live-read `reclaimAmount()` thunk for multi-section routes (lines 118-121); `settle()` flips a `done` guard and removes the abort listener so a tab-close AFTER a saved section "can no longer refund work the org already received" (lines 123-131). This is the money-safety chokepoint for every metered streaming route.

### Fold the idempotency key into the ledger ref to stop double-billing _(proposed for this repo)_

A retried or double-clicked metered request must de-duplicate against the first charge rather than billing twice, so validate the client-supplied idempotency key and fold it into the ledger reference. Scope the refund reference by user as well, or a global reference index will cross-de-duplicate two different users' reclaims.

`src/lib/ai/operation.ts:211-221` validates/bounds the idempotency key (`IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_RE`, 1-200 chars, safe charset) before using it as a ledger ref. Lines 359-371: `reclaim()` closes over a `reclaimed` flag and wraps the refund in try/catch so a ledger hiccup can neither double-refund nor escalate a serviceable mock fallback into a 500 (the charge stays debited but the user still gets a usable response — a deliberate trade-off documented inline). Mirrored at the lower layer in `src/lib/tokens/guard.ts:84-88`, which scopes the reclaim ref by user id so the ledger's global `(ref,reason)` idempotency index can't cross-dedupe two different users' reclaims.

### Write the pending-charge marker in the debit's own transaction _(proposed for this repo)_

A crash between the debit and completion leaves money taken for work never delivered unless the durability marker is written atomically with the debit itself. Write it in the same transaction, sweep stale markers periodically to refund the orphans, and run any budget-cap check inside that same transaction so the read-compute-charge race cannot open.

`src/lib/db/store.ts:462-507` — charge()'s doc: "the charge-then-reclaim durability marker (`pending_charges`) is written INSIDE this same transaction as the debit, so a crash right after the debit can never leave a debit with no marker." `recordPendingCharge`/`clearPendingCharge`/`getStalePendingCharges` form the full lease-like lifecycle. Also co-transactional budget enforcement: `ChargeBudget`/`ChargeOutcome.budgetExceeded` (store.ts:155-171) run the per-business cap check INSIDE the debit transaction, explicitly to close a read-compute-charge TOCTOU on the budget governor too.

### State whether a spend cap counts gross or net, on the money path _(proposed for this repo)_

A cap that sums gross debits while refunds are recorded outside its scope keeps a payer capped after money was returned. Either behaviour can be the right one; what is not acceptable is leaving it implicit — write the contract next to the query that computes the cap, and cite the audit that forced the choice so the next reader inherits the reasoning.

`src/lib/db/store.ts:538-553` full doc comment ending: "(Contract made explicit per the biz-ambiguity scan 2026-06-16, finding #1 — previously an undocumented silent trade-off on a money path.)" This is a repo-wide practice worth noting: several Store methods carry a named audit-finding citation (e.g. ba20bdff, 4e751c08, 16c41d94) tracing WHY a design choice was made, not just what it does.

### Declare billable operations once in a typed registry _(proposed for this repo)_

When a charge helper accepts a free-form operation string, a typo compiles and silently bills at the wrong tier — a money bug with no compile-time signal. Declare every billable operation once in a registry mapping a key to a stable persisted id and a cost tier, and type the charge helpers to accept only that union; keep the persisted ids as authored literals, since ledger history already references them.

ADR-010 (`docs/adr/ADR-010-typed-operation-registry.md:30-53`): before this, `chargeForOperation(operation: string, ...)` accepted any string and a typo like `"analyse-bill"` compiled but silently billed at the wrong/default tier — a real money bug with no compile-time signal. The registry is `as const satisfies Record<string, {id, tier}>`; `id` strings stay authored literals (not derived from the camelCase key) because they're already persisted in the ledger history. Deliberately scoped narrowly per the ADR's 'out of scope' list — it doesn't touch ledger internals or add new operations.

### Fail closed when production cannot meter or identify the caller _(proposed for this repo)_

Graceful degradation on a billable path is an open wallet: if a billable engine is configured but there is no store to meter with or no way to identify the caller, production must refuse rather than serve an unmetered anonymous call. Keep the free pass for development and keyless builds, and return the refusal reason as a typed result so each route can phrase its own rejection without re-deriving the ladder.

`src/lib/tokens/guard.ts:57-114`: `chargeForOperation` returns a discriminated union (`ok:true` with `reclaim()`, or `ok:false` with reason `unauthenticated`/`insufficient`/`misconfigured`). Comment at lines 71-79 names this explicitly as the fix for a prior footgun: 'graceful degradation = open wallet in prod'. ADR-006 (`docs/adr/ADR-006-with-charged-operation-wrapper.md`) extracts the duplicated charge→work→reclaim block that was copy-pasted across 4 routes into `withChargedOperation`, while preserving two real per-route variations (custom 401 copy, and `ingest-bill`'s reclaim-and-return-200 vs the other three's reclaim-and-rethrow). Reclaim is idempotent (keyed `reclaim:<requestId>`), so double-reclaim across the wrapper boundary is safe by construction.

### Make the charge-then-reclaim handshake durable, not in-process _(proposed for this repo)_

Metered LLM operations must write a durable pending-charge marker in the same transaction as the debit and reconcile orphans with a periodic sweep; an in-request boolean guard or an AbortSignal hook cannot refund a charge when the process dies between debit and completion.

**Why this is one shared problem**

Six member projects independently built the same charge-before-model-call ledger primitive for the same reason (an unpayable caller must never reach the model). They differ only in crash-durability of the refund path, which is not a stack or domain difference — it is the same money-correctness problem solved at different levels of durability, and one level strictly dominates.

**Current approaches**

- **Local SEO Agency** — Store.charge() atomically writes a pending_charges durability marker in the same transaction as the debit; a periodic getStalePendingCharges sweep refunds orphans left by crashes.
- **Immigration Paperwork** — In-request `reclaimed` boolean guard fires the refund exactly once on downstream failure, with a client Idempotency-Key folded into the ledger ref; nothing survives process death.
- **Grant Writing Nonprofits** — chargeOrJson() arms a once-guarded auto-reclaim on the request AbortSignal and settle() disarms it after billable work persists — covers tab-close, not crash.
- **ai-bookkeeper** — withMeteredRoute debits then calls a best-effort, idempotent reclaim() keyed by the charge ref on every failure path; r

_(evidence truncated)_

### Show tokens beside cost, and rank on cost per success _(proposed for this repo)_

Cost alone is a bad comparison axis for LLM variants: it is price-weighted, so it hides which variant is token-hungry, and providers that report no price make a real run look free. Show summed tokens beside cost, rank on cost-per-successful-outcome rather than raw spend, and render an explicit 'not tracked' when the price is unknown.

The same caveat is repeated on every aggregate type in `libs/labAggregation.ts` and `libs/evalAggregation.ts`, so it cannot be lost in a refactor:

```ts
/** Prompt + completion tokens across the group. Cost is price-weighted and
 *  hides which variant is token-hungry; a cheap model can still read most. */
totalTokens: number;
```

The table follows through — `components/versions_table/LabVersionsTable.tsx` puts both axes side by side, and refuses the false-free reading:

```ts
{!row.rating ? '—' : row.rating.costUnknown ? (
  // Ollama et al. report a hardcoded $0 — surface "not tracked" rather
  // than a misleading $0.000 that reads as "free".
  <Tooltip content={lab.vr_cost_unknown_tooltip}>...
// Cost is price-weighted, so it hides which pair is actually token-hungry —
// a cheaper model can still be the heaviest reader. Both axes, side by side.
{ key: 'tokens', ... sortFn: (a, b) => totalTokens(a) - totalTokens(b), ... }
```

## concurrency

### Stage long-running pipelines and bound every step _(proposed for this repo)_

Long-running and external-facing work drifts into one opaque function that nobody can observe, resume, or cap. Model it as named stages with an explicit bound on every dimension that can grow (rows, bytes, depth, parallelism), and make publication and instrumentation structural rather than something each writer must remember. Bounds are guesses at first, so instrument before you set them and keep the ones that depend on workload configurable.

**Practiced here:**
- CDC auto-emit — a DB update_hook publishes bus events, so a writer cannot forget to emit — engine/background.rs
- Staged build-session lifecycle (prompt → stream-json parse → gate machine → tool-test → promote) — engine/build_session
- DLQ + relay watermarking for at-least-once ingestion · storm-guard retry-count window · bounded caps on every read
- timed_query! self-instruments every repo call into a shared slow-query ring · generation-counted session handles with a Drop-guard

**Limits — when NOT to apply**

Bounds are guesses — instrument first, then set them, and make them configurable where the right value is workload-dependent. An unbounded channel behind an explicit breaker can be a legitimate choice if the reasoning is recorded.

---
*Evidence counts are synthesis estimates over the 159-finding scan corpus (16 agents, two waves), not exact joins. Full per-finding evidence lives in the scan corpus; the divergences below carry verified file:line.*

### Claim a batch with SKIP LOCKED and give each job its own transaction _(proposed for this repo)_

A queue worker that claims one row at a time serializes on latency it does not control, while one that shares a transaction across jobs turns any single failure into a batch rollback. Claim a small batch with SKIP LOCKED so parallel workers never contend, then run each job's full chain in its own transaction so concurrency is pure I/O overlap rather than shared mutable state. Make batch size, concurrency, visibility and backoff env-overridable with defaults that reproduce the previous behaviour exactly.

`crates/brainiac-pipeline/src/worker.rs:1-50` — doc + `WorkerConfig` fields each carry an inline rationale (e.g. concurrency: "pure IO-concurrency... each in-flight job holds one pool connection"). `pipeline_principal()` in `lib.rs:28-35` mints a synthetic org-scoped principal for pipeline writes, explicitly barred from end-user retrieval.

### Resume long jobs from a persisted cursor, never restart them _(proposed for this repo)_

Multi-step external-data work that runs as one long call cannot survive a crash, a deploy, or a rate limit — the whole job restarts and the same expensive reads are paid twice. Model every such job as one generic step function that reads a persisted cursor, does one bounded chunk of work, writes results and advances the cursor, so calling the same entry point again always resumes. The API surface then becomes a thin wrapper that returns the checkpoint and holds no pipeline logic of its own.

`lib/scan.ts:117-235` `stepScan(job)` dispatches to `stepDiscover/stepSeed/stepBuyers/stepRollup/stepCurate`, each of which loads/saves a `Checkpoint` row in `scan_checkpoints` (job, cursor, status, error, note). `lib/swapingest.ts:34-76` `ingestSwapStep(pair)` reuses the exact same `Checkpoint` type/table (`kind: "chain-ingest"`) for the independent chain-listening feature. The API surface is a thin resumable-step wrapper: `app/api/scan/[job]/route.ts:26-46` POST just calls `stepScan(job)` and returns the checkpoint — the route has no pipeline logic of its own.

### Beat a provider's per-call cap by chunking and accumulating locally _(proposed for this repo)_

When a provider hard-caps how much one request may return, the instinct is to negotiate a bigger call or a paid tier. The durable fix is a bounded per-call chunk size walked forward across many resumed steps, accumulating into local storage — the effective window then grows past any single call's cap instead of collapsing to it. This only works when the walk is checkpointed, so it composes with the resumable-step pattern rather than replacing it.

`lib/chain.ts:16-39` docstring and constants: `MAX_LOG_RANGE` (per-call cap, default 50), `BACKFILL_BLOCKS` (target local window, default 250, walked in `MAX_LOG_RANGE`-sized chunks). Quote: 'The fix is not a bigger single call — it is to read in small, checkpointed chunks and ACCUMULATE them into the local DuckDB store, so the window grows past the per-call cap instead of collapsing to it.' Ties directly into the resumable-pipeline pattern (`lib/swapingest.ts`) as its concrete instantiation.

### Implement rate limiting once and configure it per endpoint _(proposed for this repo)_

Rate limiting re-implemented per endpoint produces inconsistent wire contracts and a different keying mistake at each site. Put the algorithm and the rejection response in one module, make every limited endpoint a config entry naming its key (user, org, or source IP) and its window, and justify each keying choice where it is declared. State the accepted risk explicitly — in-process state is per-instance and resets on deploy — and keep the module boundary such that swapping in a shared store is a one-file change.

`limiter.ts:1-20` (ADR-0022) documents the accepted risk explicitly: in-memory state is per-instance and resets on deploy — accepted for v0 "in lieu of a paid dependency," with the module boundary chosen so a future swap to Redis/Upstash is a one-file change. Unbounded-memory risk is self-guarded: `PRUNE_AFTER_KEYS = 1024` triggers an opportunistic `pruneExpired` sweep (lines 76-88) so a growing key-space doesn't slow-leak. Keying convention is documented per-entry (lines 10-14, 33-58) e.g. `checkout:<user.id>` vs `<endpoint>:<orgId>` vs per-source-IP for unauthenticated routes — each choice justified inline (why IP vs org vs user).

### Claim shared work first-writer-wins, and release on failure _(proposed for this repo)_

Re-entrancy across a cron tick, a manual trigger and a retry is the same problem every time: two callers reach one resource and both act. Express it once as an atomic claim that writes a marker only if unclaimed or expired and returns whether this caller won, then reuse that primitive for run leases, cooldowns and notification dedupe. Every claim needs an explicit release-on-failure path, or one failed delivery leaks a permanent lock.

`src/lib/db/store.ts:576-596` — three near-identical claim/release pairs with the same doctrine documented per-call: "Stops a cron run and a manual 'Run now' ... from processing the same tenant concurrently" (acquireRunLease) and "a failed delivery RELEASES it via clearAlertSent so a later pass retries (a dropped alert is worse than a rare dup)" (markAlertSent).

### Retry only transient failures through one shared backoff wrapper _(proposed for this repo)_

Per-call-site retry loops diverge on what counts as retryable, and usually retry hard failures until the budget is gone. Route every external fetch through one wrapper that retries only transient status classes with exponential backoff and rethrows everything else immediately, using a lightweight status field on the error rather than a bespoke exception hierarchy. Make the delay function injectable so the suite exercises the retry path without sleeping.

`src/lib/retry/index.ts:1-51` — `RETRYABLE_STATUSES = new Set([429,500,502,503,504])`; `RetryOptions.delay` override "so unit tests run instantly." Errors carry a `.status` (StatusError interface, set via Object.assign in providers) that `isRetryable()` reads — a lightweight duck-typed contract shared across otherwise-unrelated provider modules instead of a custom exception hierarchy.

### Put money and lifecycle invariants in the store contract _(proposed for this repo)_

Idempotency and legal state transitions enforced by callers hold exactly until the next caller forgets. Push them into the storage interface itself — a de-dup key on the write, or a declared table of allowed from-state edges — so every driver is forced to honour the same invariant and none of them can drift. Where a trade-off is accepted (a rare duplicate beats a never-sent notification), record it at the contract, not in a commit message.

`src/lib/db/store.ts:122-127` `FEE_TRANSITION_FROM` is a single shared allowed-edge graph (`invoiced←owed`, `paid←invoiced`, `waived←owed|invoiced`) documented as shared by every driver's `transitionFee` so 'the allowed-edge graph (a money/compliance invariant) can't diverge per backend'. Similarly `credit()` de-dupes by `ref+reason` (line 270), `claimMilestoneEmail`/`releaseMilestoneEmail` (lines 329-347) implement claim-before-send at-most-once delivery with an explicit accepted trade-off documented in the comment ('releasing after a send that actually delivered could allow ONE duplicate... acceptable... never-sent is worse than a rare duplicate'), and `recordSettlementFee` (line 374-379) is idempotent per (userId, caseRef) so a re-close never overwrites an already-booked fee.

### Drain in-flight work with one shared cancellation token _(proposed for this repo)_

When each background loop polls its own shutdown flag, exit ordering is accidental: the listener stops before workers drain, or a worker claims new work after the process decided to die. Clone one cancellation token into every loop and into the HTTP server's graceful-shutdown hook, cancel it once from the signal handler, and explicitly await the worker after the listener stops. Loops should check cancellation before claiming new work but let already-running work keep its permit and finish.

`crates/server/src/main.rs:43-51` spawns a task that awaits `shutdown_signal()` then calls `shutdown.cancel()`. Worker/scheduler/janitors (lines 53-56) and `axum::serve(...).with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown.cancelled())` (lines 62-64) all share the same token. Line 66-69 explicitly awaits `worker.await` after the listener stops ("HTTP server has stopped accepting; wait for the worker to finish draining"). `worker::run` (`worker.rs:29-36`) checks `state.shutdown.cancelled()` with `biased` select before acquiring a new semaphore permit, so it stops claiming new work immediately but jobs already running keep their permits and drain naturally.

### Give every concurrently-runnable mode its own lifecycle flag _(proposed for this repo)_

One shared 'is running' boolean is fine until two modes run at once: cancelling one clears the wrong flag, or clears a flag a live run still needs, and the UI stays wedged until restart. Declare the state machine once and instantiate it per mode so legal transitions live in one place while the instances stay independent. Pin it with a concurrency regression test — start several modes, cancel one, assert the others are untouched — because a per-mode test passes even with a shared flag.

`src/stores/__tests__/labSlice.cancel.test.ts` documents the shipped bug and guards the fix:

> Regression we're guarding against: cancelArena used to call `labLifecycle.markCancelled` (legacy `isLabRunning`) instead of the per-mode lifecycle, leaving `isArenaRunning` stuck at true (cancel button stayed visible, launch button stayed disabled, persona orbit dot never cleared until app restart).

The decisive test is the concurrency one — start Matrix, A/B and Eval, cancel A/B, assert the other two flags are still `true`. A per-mode test alone would pass even with a shared flag.

The underlying state machine is declared once in `src/lib/fsm.ts` (`runLifecycleFSM`: `idle → running → {failed, cancelled, finished, timed_out} → idle|running`) and instantiated per mode, so "which transitions are legal" is defined in one place while the *instances* are independent. `createFSM` pre-compiles the transition table into Sets and offers both a throwing `transition` and a logging `tryTransition`.

### Snapshot the target entity id before an await and re-check after _(proposed for this repo)_

In an editor over a selectable entity, every setter implicitly targets whatever is selected now, so any async hop lets the user switch entities in the gap and the write lands on the wrong record. Capture the id before the first await and bail on every resume where the live store no longer matches; for undo entries, carry a token captured at record time and check it on both sides of the call. Read the live store rather than a closure flag, since an effect that nulls its own dependency mid-flight will fire cleanup on the wrong trigger.

`src/features/agents/sub_editor/libs/useEditorSave.ts` does this three ways:

```ts
const savePersonaId = selectedPersonaId;
await applyPersonaOp(savePersonaId, op);
if (useAgentStore.getState().selectedPersona?.id !== savePersonaId) return;
setBaseline(...); pushUndo(...);
```

Undo entries go further and carry a token captured at record time (`capturePersonaToken(personaId)` → `token.isStillCurrent()` checked both before and after the IPC), because "pressing Ctrl+Z after switching personas … would write persona A's old field values into persona B's draft+baseline, silently corrupting B and lying that 'All saved'".

`src/features/agents/sub_design/libs/useDesignTabState.ts` applies the same discipline to a multi-minute LLM compile, and adds a subtlety: the guard reads the **live store** rather than a cleanup-set closure flag, because the effect nulls one of its own deps mid-flight and a cleanup flag fired on its own trigger consumption ("auto-start silently no-oped, leaving an orphaned conversation row per attempt"). It also deletes the conversation row it created when the check fails.

### Diff a serialized autosave against the in-flight snapshot _(proposed for this repo)_

Serializing overlapping autosaves by awaiting the in-flight promise invites a 'nothing changed, skip' short-circuit that compares the live draft to the baseline — but the baseline is updated through render state and lags the await, so edits made during the await get swallowed. Store the exact snapshot handed to the running save synchronously in a ref and short-circuit only when the live draft still equals that snapshot. Clear the refs only when they still point at the save that is finishing, so a queued successor is not torn down by its predecessor.

`src/features/agents/sub_editor/libs/useDebouncedSaveGroup.ts` keeps `inFlightRef` (the promise) *and* `inFlightSnapshotRef` (the draft passed to it):

```ts
while (inFlightRef.current) {
  const snapshotBefore = inFlightSnapshotRef.current;
  await inFlightRef.current;
  if (snapshotBefore && !draftChanged(draftRef.current, snapshotBefore, keys)) return;
}
```

The comment records the regression verbatim: "Previously we compared against baselineRef, which is updated via setBaseline (async) — that left a window where the ref still pointed at the *previous* baseline and the early-return swallowed unsaved edits." The `finally` also only clears the refs when they still point at *this* promise, so a queued successor isn't torn down by its predecessor.

### Block double-submit with a synchronous ref, only for async handlers _(proposed for this repo)_

A reactive loading or disabled flag cannot stop a fast double-click, because the click event is dispatched synchronously before the re-render commits. Set an in-flight ref at click time, block subsequent clicks while it is set, and clear it in a finally so a thrown action stays retryable. Engage the guard only when the handler returns a thenable, or rapid-click controls like steppers and paginators stop firing every click.

`src/features/shared/components/buttons/Button.tsx`:

```ts
// Double-submit guard — only engages when `onClick` returns a thenable (i.e. an async
// handler). The native click event is dispatched synchronously, so a fast double-click
// can fire twice before React commits a reactive `loading`/`disabled` re-render.
const result = onClick(e);
if (result != null && typeof result.then === 'function') {
  inFlightRef.current = true;
  void Promise.resolve(result).finally(() => { inFlightRef.current = false; });
}
```

`AsyncButton.tsx` extends it: a **synchronous throw** releases the guard before rethrowing (so a failed action can be retried), and while in flight it drives its own `internalLoading` so the spinner is right even when the caller never threads `isLoading`.

`ConfirmDialog.tsx` applies the same idea at dialog level — while `onConfirm()` is pending it disables both buttons *and* ignores backdrop/Escape dismissal *"so the action cannot be fired twice (double-click, trackpad bounce, impatient retry)"*, re-enabling in `finally` so a thrown action stays retryable.
